clue.text: Spotted son getting kissed, with lips initially closed

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son

indicators.note: something closed in is shut inside, so that letter goes within the word for kissed

parts.note: a peck is a quick kiss

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows

parts.note: the first letter of lips

explanation.surface: A boy is caught kissing, his lips kept politely shut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' looks like 'seen', but it means marked with spots. The lips' letter is shut inside the kiss word just before its ending.
explanation.definitionFit: Speckled describes a surface covered in small spots or flecks, so it is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Northern town offering safe shelter from wind

parts.note: peter is old criminal slang for a safe
the lee is the sheltered side, away from the wind

explanation.surface: A town in the north promises refuge from the weather.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter for a safe is old underworld slang that crosswords still use; Peterlee is a new town in County Durham, in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Peterlee is a real town in County Durham, in the north of England, so it is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Giant dog that is straying across mountain in Greece

indicators.note: lying across something means spanning it on both sides, so what remains of the dog wraps round the mountain
something straying wanders off, so those letters leave the word for the dog

parts.note: a collie is a breed of sheepdog
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is
Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly

explanation.surface: A huge stray dog is crossing a Greek peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' looks like a noun for an ogre, but it is the adjective; 'that is' is the Latin abbreviation that strays from the dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are adjectives for something enormous in size, so giant is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Bread and veg?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a shaped mass of baked bread
second meaning: to idle about doing nothing, as in veg out

explanation.walkthrough: Bread and veg look like a shopping list; veg here is the slang verb for lazing about, and the question mark flags that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaf is a unit of baked bread, and to loaf is to idle, which is what vegging out means.

clue.text: English resort beset by mostly terrible gloom

indicators.note: to be beset is to be surrounded on all sides, so the resort sits inside the other word
mostly means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: dire means terrible or dreadful
E is the abbreviation for English
a spa is a resort town with mineral springs

explanation.surface: An English seaside resort is surrounded by awful, miserable weather.
explanation.walkthrough: DIRE loses its last letter to give DIR, which then holds E and SPA: D-ESPA-IR.
explanation.definitionFit: Despair is utter hopelessness, a deeper shade of the dark low mood that gloom describes.

clue.text: Newspaper with a preoccupation about British holidaymakers' activity?

indicators.note: about means going around, so the preoccupation wraps round the abbreviation

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
to have a thing about something is to be preoccupied with it
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: A tabloid obsesses over what British tourists get up to abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: A THING goes round B, which then follows SUN. The question mark admits the definition is one example of what holidaymakers do.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying in the sun on a beach is a typical pastime of people on holiday, so it is an example.

clue.text: Meat pie not unknown to friend abroad

indicators.note: algebra's unknowns are x, y and z, so 'not unknown' drops one of those letters

parts.note: a pie is a pastry dish
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: Someone abroad is offered a meat pie as a gift for a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meat pie' reads as one thing, but meat alone is the definition. In algebra x, y and z are the unknowns, so one of them is lost.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is seasoned, smoked cured beef, so it is a particular kind of meat.

clue.text: Almost spring — hours of darkness becoming shorter

indicators.note: becoming shorter means losing its final letter

parts.note: a spring is a natural source of water, as is a well
the night is the dark part of the day

explanation.surface: With spring nearly here, the nights are drawing in less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost spring' looks like one phrase about the season, but almost alone is the definition and spring is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-nigh is an old-fashioned adverb meaning very nearly, so it can replace almost directly.

clue.text: Queen wants single attendant at rear of the carriage

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of the
QU is a recognised abbreviation for queen
I is the Roman numeral for one
a page is a young attendant or servant

explanation.surface: A queen needs a lone footman to ride at the back of her coach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attendant at rear of the carriage' wants to be a footman; carriage alone is the definition, and the rear of 'the' supplies the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An equipage is a horse-drawn carriage with its horses and attendants, so it is a grand kind of carriage.

clue.text: Largely musty bars in English city

indicators.note: largely means most of it, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: stale means musty, no longer fresh
to bar something is to ban it

explanation.surface: Most of the pubs in an English cathedral city smell stale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs, but it is the verb meaning prohibits.
explanation.definitionFit: St Albans is a cathedral city in Hertfordshire, just north of London, so it is an example of an English city.

clue.text: Local alert put out concerning young teenager

parts.note: a local is the pub nearest your home

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or upset, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood warning goes out about a young adolescent.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain your local is the pub you regularly drink at.
explanation.definitionFit: Pubertal is the adjective for puberty, the stage of early adolescence, so it means relating to a young teen.

clue.text: Start to get disorientated, going round country in shiny coat

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter of get

indicators.note: going round means surrounding, so the word for disorientated encircles the country

parts.note: someone disorientated does not know where they are
a European country

explanation.surface: A traveller loses their bearings touring a country, dressed in something glossy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coat' suggests clothing, but it is a layer of paint.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloss paint dries to a high shine, and a coat is a layer of paint, so it is a shiny coat.

clue.text: Sound of drums making row, drowning broadcaster briefly

indicators.note: something drowning is plunged under, so the shortened broadcaster sinks inside the word for row

parts.note: to paddle a boat is to row it

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the radio broadcasts

explanation.surface: Drumming makes such a din that it drowns out the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a noisy quarrel next to drums, but it is the boating verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A paradiddle is a basic drumming pattern played with alternating sticks, and the word imitates its sound.

clue.text: Land captured by Somalians

indicators.note: captured by means held inside, so the answer sits within the next word

parts.note: letters three to six of the word

explanation.surface: Territory seized by Somali fighters.
explanation.definitionFit: Mali is a West African country, and land is a general word for a country or nation.

clue.text: Secure command in absence of first officer

indicators.note: with its first letter absent, the word begins one letter later

parts.note: to seal something is to close it securely
to give the word is to give the command

explanation.surface: Taking control while the first officer is away from the bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First officer' looks like one phrase, but first belongs to the deletion and officer alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sea Lord is a senior naval officer on Britain's Admiralty Board, so he is a kind of officer.

clue.text: Seafood's hot and full of sauce?

parts.note: scampi are breaded langoustines, plus the 's
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: Spicy shellfish swimming in sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: Sauce looks like the dressing on the seafood, but it is cheek; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauce is cheekiness, and someone scampish behaves like a scamp, a cheeky rascal, so they are impudent.

clue.text: A US officer arrests Greek character ignoring the law

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to arrest is to take into custody, so the officer holds the character inside

parts.note: a narc is an American narcotics agent
chi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: An American cop arrests a Greek lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The arrest suits the lawless surface; NARC is the officer and opens to take CHI.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchic means lacking order or control, as in rejecting the rule of law.

clue.text: Ineffective politician is besieged by women's group at end of speech

indicators.note: a besieged town is surrounded on every side, so the following words wrap round

parts.note: the WI is the Women's Institute

indicators.note: 'end of' keeps only the last letter of 'speech'

parts.note: the final letter of speech
a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A feeble MP is surrounded by the Women's Institute at the end of a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: MP and IS are besieged on both sides by WI and the H ending speech. The WI is the Women's Institute, a British community organisation for women.
explanation.definitionFit: Wimpish means feeble and timid like a wimp, so it describes someone who has no effect.

clue.text: With one type of bread, new chef regularly used very little dough

parts.note: pitta is a flat bread
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first and third letters of chef

explanation.surface: A cook uses only a scrap of dough for flatbread.
explanation.walkthrough: Dough looks like the baker's sort, but it is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Dough is slang for money, and a pittance is a very small, inadequate sum of it.

clue.text: Discharge small rifle

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
to rifle is to ransack or plunder

explanation.surface: Firing off a little gun.
explanation.walkthrough: Discharge and rifle together suggest firing a gun; rifle is the verb for ransacking.
explanation.definitionFit: A spillage is liquid that has escaped from a container, which is a discharge.

clue.text: Travel at speed, as Spooner might have said, in this display?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was known for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so the pair is swapped

parts.note: to ply is to travel regularly, as a ferry plies a route, and fast means at speed: ply fast

explanation.surface: A spectator describes aircraft streaking overhead, in the muddled words of the Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as Spooner might have said' asks for a Spoonerism: say 'ply fast' with its opening P and F sounds exchanged and you hear the answer, which is also what the aircraft in the display do.
explanation.definitionFit: A flypast is a ceremonial display in which aircraft fly low in formation over a crowd or venue.

clue.text: Healthy meal sent back unfinished, sadly

indicators.note: sent back means returned, so the word is read in the other direction
unfinished means missing its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a salad is a healthy meal

explanation.surface: Sadly, a diner returns a half-eaten salad.
explanation.definitionFit: Alas is an exclamation of sorrow, used as an interjection where one might say sadly.

clue.text: Enjoys things ordered at food store

parts.note: a delicatessen

indicators.note: ordered means arranged or sorted, so these letters are set out afresh

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopper relishes ordering treats at the delicatessen.
explanation.walkthrough: The deli comes first in the answer although the clue names it last.
explanation.definitionFit: To delight in something is to take great pleasure in it, which is what enjoys means.

clue.text: Ready for a holiday, stopped working

definitions.meaning: first meaning: with the suitcases all filled
second meaning: broke down, as a machine does

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one worker who has finished and is off on holiday; the phrase splits into two separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Packed up means both having your bags packed to go away and, informally, breaking down or ceasing to function.

clue.text: Grace's final word is mean, to boot

indicators.note: to boot is read as giving a kick, and a kicked word gets knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Grace is said to end on a stingy note as well.
explanation.walkthrough: To boot normally means also; here it is read literally as kicking the word around.
explanation.definitionFit: Grace is a prayer said before a meal, and prayers traditionally close with the word amen.

clue.text: Soldiers in area west of Iran garbled language

indicators.note: in an across answer, west of means placed to the left of what follows

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: in places the soldiers inside the mixed-up letters
garbled means jumbled and confused, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
soldiers are the men of an army

explanation.surface: Troops in a region bordering Iran speak a muddled tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldiers go inside the jumbled country rather than inside the area, which stands alone at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Armenian is the Indo-European language spoken in Armenia, so it is an example of a language.

clue.text: Manhattan cocktails a disappointment to the French

parts.note: a swizz is British slang for a swindle or letdown
les is French for the, plural

explanation.surface: French drinkers find New York's cocktails a letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: A swizz is schoolchild British slang for something unfairly disappointing.
explanation.definitionFit: A swizzle is a frothy mixed drink stirred with a swizzle stick, so it is a kind of cocktail, here with a US flavour.

clue.text: With quite a few diamonds and two queens, I'll make a bid

parts.note: ten is a fair number
D is the abbreviation for diamonds in card games
ER, Elizabeth Regina, twice

explanation.surface: A bridge player holding plenty of diamonds and a pair of queens decides to bid.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge surface makes bid look like a card call; the definition is spoken by the person bidding for a contract.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenderer is someone who puts in a tender, a formal offer or bid for a contract.
